themes.name: Compile-green is not done — verify runtime end-to-end
themes.description: User repeatedly rejects 'cargo check passed' / 'pnpm check passed' as a definition of done; success is the running app demonstrating the behavior, with files actually moved/symlinked, models actually loaded, windows actually rendered.
themes.underlying_need: Stop being lied to about progress; the unit of trust is observable behavior in the running binary, not green lints. Repeated 'compile-green' claims followed by an unbootable app is what destroyed trust.
automatic_actions: After any change that affects runtime, explicitly state 'compile-green; not runtime-verified' instead of claiming it works
List the specific click-by-click verification the user needs to perform when they next launch the app
Run `cargo check -p devpulse_desktop_backend` (the binary crate) — never just the library crate
Include `pnpm check`, biome, lefthook in the verification cycle, not only cargo
When the app is supposed to load a model / spawn a sidecar / open a window, treat that as the success criterion, not the build exit code
Surface windows-specific runtime concerns (DLLs, sccache, file locks) before declaring done
anti_patterns: Reporting 'all gates pass' or 'ready' based on typecheck or biome alone
Skipping the binary crate by checking only library crates
Claiming a feature works without ever launching the app
Treating absence of red errors as presence of working behavior
Saying 'should work' when the code path was never executed
Listing what was authored as if it were what was verified
example_paraphrases: The compile passed but where is my UI? Nothing renders — that means it isn't done.
Stop telling me it works because cargo check returned zero. I never saw the model load.
You verified with checks, not by actually clicking through the wizard end to end.

themes.name: No stubs, no half-finished progress, no fake completion
themes.description: User detects and rejects stub buttons, TODO placeholders, silent no-op IPC handlers, partial rewrites left mid-flight, and reverts disguised as fixes. Either the work is real and complete, or the gap is acknowledged plainly.
themes.underlying_need: Predictable trust that what is shipped is whole. Stubs and silent reverts are read as deception, not as iteration. The user would rather hear 'this is a multi-hour task' than see disabled buttons.
automatic_actions: Before finishing a file, audit every code path: real work, or honest error explaining why not — nothing in between
Feature-gate optional work behind a cargo feature so the disabled state is explicit, not pretend
When work cannot be completed in scope, state the gap directly with the reason and the time estimate
Never ship a UI control that does not call a real verb; remove the control instead
If a Tauri command exists in name only, return a structured 'not enabled' error, not Ok(())
After deleting/refactoring, restate what was absorbed where so the user can verify the move
anti_patterns: Disabled buttons with 'coming soon' / 'wire this later'
Files containing only `//! TODO: implement`
Tauri verbs that silently return Ok with no work
Reverting a change without telling the user, then pretending it's still in
Listing 'authored' files as evidence of progress when none of them run
Mid-bulk-rename leaving a partially renamed tree
example_paraphrases: Booting with a pile of stubs is not a baseline, it's theater.
Don't claim it's done — half the buttons are wired to nothing.
If the model loader can't load a model, say so; don't ship a fake import button.

themes.name: Research first, then EXECUTE — no infinite planning
themes.description: User wants the planning skill / research notes / SSOT mapping done before writing code, but only as a precursor to actually executing. They reject planning loops where research repeats and code never lands.
themes.underlying_need: Disciplined sequence — read existing code, write findings to disk, get owner sign-off on forks, then ship. Avoid both (a) writing code without reading the codebase and (b) producing endless plans with no execution.
automatic_actions: Open the planning skill / write a research doc to disk before non-trivial implementation
Map SSOTs first: list every place a concept already lives, flag duplicates
Surface STOP points as one-line questions, not multi-option decision matrices
After plan approval, execute the plan — do not commit infrastructure docs as if they were the work
If research uncovers a blocking compile error or a broken foundation, fix that BEFORE the new feature
Tag each plan section with the file paths it will touch so the owner can audit scope
anti_patterns: Writing 5 plans without shipping a single feature
Re-researching what was already decided last session
Producing decision-tree proposals when a one-line confirm would do
Researching forever to avoid executing on something hard
Skipping the read-the-actual-files step and inferring from filenames
Treating documented architecture as already-existing on disk without verifying
example_paraphrases: Stay in planning, write the research notes to disk, get this clean before you touch code.
You've planned for hours — go execute the plan, that was the agreement.
I don't want another plan, I want the broken foundation fixed first.

themes.name: All warnings — including non-fatal and pre-existing — get fixed
themes.description: When the user says 'check' they mean every diagnostic the toolchain emits: clippy notes, missing-docs warnings, dead-code warnings, SD5 build notes, biome warnings, lefthook notes. Pre-existing warnings on a touched file are owned by the touch.
themes.underlying_need: Clean toolchain output as proof the change is finished and the work is craftsmanship-grade. Residual warnings read as 'rushed.'
automatic_actions: Run `cargo check --all-targets --message-format=short` for both engine and desktop_backend to catch lib-test warnings
Run `pnpm check` and confirm 0 errors AND 0 warnings
Run `pnpm ds:tokens:build` and read SD5 build notes
On a touched file, fix every pre-existing warning in that file too
For feature-gated code, guard imports with matching #[cfg] / #[cfg_attr(not(feature), allow(dead_code))]
Report each warning category cleared, not just 'all green'
anti_patterns: Reporting '0 errors' while warnings remain
Skipping `--all-targets` and missing test-only warnings
Treating 'pre-existing' as an excuse to leave warnings in a touched file
Adding `#[allow]` instead of fixing the cause
Ignoring SD5 build notes about filtered references
example_paraphrases: All warnings, every note, every non-fatal — fix them all, no exceptions.
Don't tell me clean while clippy is still emitting on the file you just edited.
Specta notes count too. Read the output.

themes.name: One source of truth — Rust kernel owns it, UI consumes it
themes.description: User repeatedly demands that a concept (config, slot definition, vocabulary, terminology, hardware tier, dev profile) live in exactly one place — typically the Rust kernel — and have other layers consume via codegen or vocabulary translation, never via parallel duplicates.
themes.underlying_need: A clean contract where the Rust side owns canonical state and the frontend reads via generated types. Removes drift, removes 'find/replace across N files,' and makes IP boundary work as a vocabulary layer rather than parallel DTOs.
automatic_actions: Before adding a type/enum/string label, search for an existing definition in kernel/clyffy or engine and reuse it
When a kernel type needs to cross IPC, derive `specta::Type` on the kernel type — do not create an engine DTO mirror
Use the existing vocabulary registry (ip_term!, surface!) for layman-facing labels
Run `cargo xtask regen-bindings` whenever a Rust type changes shape
Flag any duplicate storage of the same concept (preferences.json + libSQL + SurrealDB) as a STOP point
When asked to add a UI label, register it in the YAML/registry first, then consume the generated const
anti_patterns: `pub struct FooDto { ... } impl From<KernelFoo> for FooDto`
Hardcoding a string label in a Svelte file when a registered surface const exists
Adding a third storage location for an already-duplicated concept
Writing a parallel enum with the same variants for IPC
Maintaining synced copies of the same model list in Rust and TS
example_paraphrases: Rust is the source of truth — the UI reads what Rust says, period.
Stop creating wrappers; rename through the vocabulary registry instead.
If we update the source of truth, the bindings should update — that's the whole point of the codegen.

themes.name: Model loader / AI UI requirements are LOCKED — stop redebating
themes.description: Recurring pattern of the user re-stating identical product requirements about the model loader (Qwen as floor, Harrier 0.5B downloaded+scanned, brain-discovers/UI-simplifies, click=full-model on-demand, HF browse as its own overlay, blue tint, animated background, layman-friendly, fluid clamp).
themes.underlying_need: Stop having the same fight every session. The product spec exists; honor it. When ambiguity remains, surface the conflict against the locked spec rather than silently re-interpret.
automatic_actions: Before touching any model-loader / AI-picker / HF-browse / runtime-config UI, re-read project_model_loader_requirements.md
Map the proposed change against the locked points before implementing
Use blue palette for primary CTAs on AI surfaces — never grayscale
Treat full-model load as the default click action; never partial / preview
Layout uses XY fluid clamp on first-page typography and spacing
If the proposal conflicts with the locked spec, STOP and surface the conflict to the user
anti_patterns: Suggesting 0.6B as Clyffy's main brain (4B floor)
Embedding HF browse inline in the main picker
Shipping a black-and-white wizard / model-loader
Loading a slice / preview on click instead of the full model
Asking again whether Qwen should be the floor
Hardcoding rem/px on landing-page typography
example_paraphrases: We have already decided this — Qwen is the floor, click loads the entire model, HF browse is its own overlay.
I gave you the colors and the blue tint — why is the wizard still grayscale?
Brain discovers, UI simplifies — the layman never sees a quant filename.

themes.name: Design system discipline — semantic tokens, SD5 transforms, no raw values
themes.description: User holds the line on Tier 2 semantic tokens (primary/danger/accent), SD5 built-in transforms (oklch / fluid clamp via fluidDimensionToClamp), no raw hex/rgb in components, no preset-lookup tables, no per-surface palette names like variant="wizard".
themes.underlying_need: A coherent visual system the user can re-skin from one Tier-2 binding without touching components. Drift from this contract (variant="blue", preset registries, hand-written hex) breaks the visual editor story.
automatic_actions: Components read `var(--accent-primary-*)` / `var(--surface-*)` — never hex or palette names
When a brand color is needed, add it to the SD5 source JSON and let the built-in transform produce the oklch ramp
Use fluid clamp tokens for typography and spacing on first-run / setup surfaces
Variant names are intent (`primary`, `danger`, `muted`) — never palette (`blue`) or surface (`wizard`)
Components are base-+-style: base owns ARIA, variants only add styling
Run `pnpm ds:tokens:build` after token edits and read the build notes
anti_patterns: `color: #17deef` in a component file
`variant="wizard"` or `variant="blue"` props
Custom oklch transforms when SD5 has a built-in
renderForge preset-key indirection between component and tokens
Variants re-implementing ARIA instead of inheriting from base
Per-surface CSS files that bake a scope into the token vocabulary
example_paraphrases: Use the built-in SD5 oklch transform — stop writing custom transforms.
Tokens are tier-2 semantic; the component never knows the palette name.
Base component owns ARIA; the variant only paints.

themes.name: Honest, real-time UI state — runes reflect the Rust truth
themes.description: User insists on transparent live state at all times: VRAM usage, GPU resources, slot statuses, download progress per shard, system info — all rune-driven from real Tauri events, never hardcoded mock numbers, never silent loading.
themes.underlying_need: Trust through visibility. If the backend is doing something, the UI says so live. If it isn't, the UI doesn't pretend.
automatic_actions: Wire Rust LoaderEventSink → Tauri app.emit → frontend listener for every long operation
Use `$state` / `$derived` runes; subscribe via `createTauriEvent` or equivalent
Show per-shard progress for SafeTensors (1-of-7), per-file progress for downloads, friendly speeds and ETAs
When backend reports unknown / zero, show 'unknown' or 'not reported' — never fabricate
Cancel buttons are wired to real Rust verbs that abort the operation
Status pills / health badges read from health-poll runes, not local timers
anti_patterns: Hardcoded VRAM numbers in a wizard preset
Spinner that never resolves because the event is never emitted
30-minute timeouts triggered because completion event was never bridged
UI labels saying 'Ready' before the rune confirms it
Mocked GPU info when the real backend value is empty
example_paraphrases: The bar should read whatever Rust says right now — not a placeholder.
If you can't get a real progress event, don't show a fake bar.
Make sure the download-complete event is bridged — the spinner has been spinning for 30 minutes.

themes.name: WAI-ARIA APG-compliant base components — variants inherit, never duplicate
themes.description: User wants a single base-component family tree (display / inputs / interaction / navigation / overlays) with strict WAI-ARIA APG compliance held in the base. Variants are styling-only descendants; they never re-author ARIA, keyboard handling, or focus management.
themes.underlying_need: Accessibility-by-construction without duplication. Every variant inherits correct ARIA from one tested base; the design system stays small and auditable.
automatic_actions: When asked for a variant, write it as a styling-only wrapper around the existing base
Confirm or extend the base's ARIA wiring before authoring a variant — never duplicate ARIA
Use the established families/{display,inputs,interaction,navigation,overlays} folder shape with one master barrel
Co-locate types per family (types.ts) and re-export through the family index.ts
Reuse react-aria-components primitives where they already cover the role
Cite the APG pattern being implemented in the base component's docstring
anti_patterns: Variant component re-implementing keyboard handlers the base already has
Two competing tooltip / dialog implementations in different folders
Master index.ts containing everything inline instead of barrel-of-barrels
Skipping APG roles because 'it works visually'
New component that bypasses the base and goes straight to raw HTML for styling reasons
example_paraphrases: Variants only paint — ARIA lives in the base, period.
Get the families organized: display, inputs, interaction, navigation, overlays.
If react-aria-components covers it, use it; don't reinvent the keyboard wiring.

themes.name: Paste of build/lint failure — diagnose root cause and fix all of it
themes.description: User pastes raw cargo / pnpm / lefthook / biome / sccache / linker output (often huge, including warnings, exit codes, transcript paths) and expects a complete root-cause analysis plus a fix that clears every diagnostic in the paste.
themes.underlying_need: The paste IS the prompt — the user wants the failure read carefully (every error, every warning, every note), the root cause identified, and a concrete fix that addresses ALL diagnostics, not just the first error.
automatic_actions: Read the entire paste — every error, every warning, every note, every exit-code
Identify the chain: which stage failed, which crate, which line, what type / trait was missing
Group errors by root cause (one missing trait derive often explains 5 errors)
Fix the root, not just the surface — derive the missing trait, don't `#[allow]` past it
Address every warning the paste includes (see `all-warnings` mode)
Surface adjacent root causes the user might not have asked about (DLL paths, sccache access denied, file locks)
anti_patterns: Reading only the first error and stopping
Suggesting `#[allow(dead_code)]` instead of using the field
Asking the user what they pasted means before reading it
Fixing one error and reporting done while three more are in the paste
Skipping the warnings section because it's 'not fatal'
Speculating from filename without opening the file referenced in the diagnostic
example_paraphrases: Here is what cargo printed — explain why and fix every error and warning in this paste.
Linker is failing on the DLL path — read the whole transcript, not just the last 5 lines.
process didn't exit successfully — figure out which stage actually failed.

themes.name: Don't rush foundational work — best practice, no shortcuts, senior-dev discipline
themes.description: User repeatedly demands enterprise / senior-dev grade for foundational layers (xtask observability, service lifecycle, graceful shutdown, structured logging, integration tests). Rejects bandaids and shortcut workarounds even when they unblock a build.
trigger_phrases: as a real rust engineer would
themes.underlying_need: The platform has years of investment behind it — foundations need to be sturdy, not patched. Senior-dev discipline (no println in xtask, structured tracing, integration tests, decomposed functions, real lifecycle management) is the baseline.
automatic_actions: On foundational code (xtask, services, lifecycle, telemetry): use `tracing` with structured fields, not println/eprintln
Decompose long functions; flag `#[allow(clippy::too_many_lines)]` as a code smell
Add integration tests (not just unit) for cross-module behavior
Implement graceful-then-forced shutdown patterns with retry windows on shutdown
Use `BufWriter` + atomic writes for file I/O; never silently `let _ =` on errors
Distinct exit codes for distinct failure modes so CI / orchestrators can branch
anti_patterns: println!/eprintln! in production-scope orchestrators
Catch-all exit-code 1 for every failure
Substring matching on tool output as a stable contract
Silent error swallowing (`let _ = writeln!`)
Skipping a real installer pipeline (NSIS/WIX) by zipping a folder and calling it portable
Force-killing services without a graceful attempt
example_paraphrases: A senior Rust engineer would not ship this — decompose it, structure the logs, write the integration test.
Stop sidestepping the installer; we want NSIS first then WIX — do this right.
On shutdown, attempt graceful three times over 30 seconds, then force; never just kill.

themes.name: Pre-release mode — align now, no backcompat, no migration questions
themes.description: User refuses to entertain backcompat / migration / grandfathering questions. The project is unreleased; the answer is always 'replace, align, no shims.'
themes.underlying_need: Move at full speed. The repo is private and unreleased; carrying old shapes only slows execution. When the user pivots, the old version disappears.
automatic_actions: Never ask 'how should we handle existing X?' — replace it
Frame migration work as 'I'll align existing X to the new shape' (statement, not question)
Delete legacy code paths when their replacement lands; do not leave deprecation aliases
When the user reverts a typed direction, treat it as if it never happened — no archive note
Save question budget for genuine forks (format, ownership, strictness modes), not migration logistics
anti_patterns: Asking 'should we keep the old API for backcompat?'
Adding `_v2` suffixes when the v1 will be replaced
Leaving deprecated re-exports 'for safety'
Authoring a migration script for unreleased internal data
Treating prior session's decisions as immutable when the user has reversed them
example_paraphrases: There is no backwards compat — I haven't released; align it now.
Don't ask about old data — delete the old shape and move on.
If I reverted that direction, drop it as if it never existed.

themes.name: Direct action — no preamble, no apology, no narration
themes.description: User wants the response to start with the work. No 'Great question!' opener, no 'I understand your frustration,' no restating the request, no summarizing tool output verbatim. Status updates are one line.
themes.underlying_need: Maximum signal-per-word. The user reads diffs and tool output directly; narration is friction. When they're frustrated, acknowledgement-of-frustration is read as more friction, not empathy.
automatic_actions: Open with the action / finding, not with a greeting or restatement
When frustrated, extract the technical need and act — do not apologize
End-of-turn summary is one line: what changed, what's open
When the user is wrong, correct firmly and directly with the reason
Skip 'Let me start by reading…' / 'I'll now…' phrasing — just do it
Suppress emotional acknowledgement unless the user explicitly asks for it
anti_patterns: Opening with 'I understand you're frustrated'
Restating the user's request before answering
'Great point!' / 'Good catch!' style affirmations
Multi-paragraph apology for prior session's errors
Narrating each tool call as you make it
Asking permission before doing something the user just told you to do
example_paraphrases: Stop the preamble — get to the work.
Don't apologize, just fix it.
I told you go, so go — no clarifying questions.
